performers: Skidmore College Orchestra, per the Free Music Archive and Internet Archive; not named on the Commons page
question: How does an orchestra turn a clock and a flying witch into the same piece?
intro: Baba Yaga’s hut stands on chicken legs and her mortar flies. A fast, wild first part, a very quiet slower middle and a return are followed, without a break, by the Great Gate. Instruments named here follow Ravel’s orchestration, the probable but undocumented version.

sections.label: The wild music returns
sections.mNote: strident brass material returns after a forceful chord

cues.title: Earthy rushes and shrieks
cues.text: Earthy, quick-moving ideas are contrasted with high-pitched interjections. The level rises from about −20 dB to −12 dB within twenty seconds, at two to three detected attacks a second.
cues.evidence: Quick earthy ideas and high-pitched interjections: Philharmonia guide (Joanna Wyld). Relative level −19.7 dB (0:00), −12.3 dB (0:20); onsets per second 2.2, 2.6, 2.8, 3.2, 2.4 at 0:00–0:20.

cues.title: A strident trumpet theme
cues.text: A strident trumpet theme is followed by competing brass blasts, decorated by the urgent orchestral texture. By 0:35 the sound is at its brightest in this section, about 2,000 Hz.
cues.evidence: Strident trumpet theme and competing brass blasts: Philharmonia guide. Brightness 1,331 Hz (0:25), 1,608 Hz (0:30), 2,008 Hz (0:35), 1,737 Hz (0:40); boundaries at 0:30 and 0:42 (novelty 0.42, 0.41). The report does not identify instruments.

cues.title: The floor falls away
cues.text: At about 1:09 the strongest boundary arrives and the sound collapses by more than twenty decibels, from about −12 dB to −35 dB within four seconds. This is the slower, hushed middle section the title calls Andante mosso.
cues.evidence: Boundary at 1:08 (novelty 1.00); a 1-second pass gives −11.8 dB at 1:08, −24.2 dB at 1:09, −30.5 dB at 1:10 and −35.4 dB at 1:12; the 5-second table shows −13.0 dB (1:05) and −33.6 dB (1:10), staying near −26 to −34 dB to 2:25. The Andante mosso marking is in the movement title.

cues.title: A clock shaped like a hut
cues.text: Hartmann designed a clock in the form of Baba Yaga’s hut on hen’s legs; Steinberg describes a metal fourteenth-century style clock with cocks’ heads. Only the sketch survives. Mussorgsky added the witch’s flight in a mortar, and the rhythm recalls ticking.
cues.evidence: Michael Steinberg’s Boston Symphony note (clock in the style of the fourteenth century, shaped like a hut with cocks’ heads, metal; Baba Yaga in her mortar) and Peter Laki’s Cleveland Orchestra note (clock design survives only as a sketch; rhythm recalls ticking). Related edge: hartmann-pictures--mussorgsky-pictures-1874. The note sits in the hush (−33 dB at 1:30).

cues.title: The witches’ sabbath again
cues.text: Mussorgsky had already written a witches’ sabbath: St John’s Night on the Bare Mountain, finished 23 June 1867 and refused by Balakirev. Orrin Howard hears in Baba Yaga “Mussorgsky’s best Bald Mountain pictorialism”.
cues.evidence: The 1867 completion date and Balakirev’s refusal: site influence edge mussorgsky-bald-mountain--rimsky-korsakov-edition-1886 (content/influence/romantic.json); the quotation: LA Phil note by Orrin Howard (https://www.laphil.com/works/pictures-at-an-exhibition-modest-mussorgsky-zs2phpn9). The note sits in the hush (−26.0 to −29.2 dB, 1:55–2:10).

cues.title: A forceful chord
cues.text: At about 2:28 the level jumps by roughly seventeen decibels within three seconds: a forceful orchestral chord announces the return of the strident material. The long hush is over.
cues.evidence: A 1-second pass gives −34.1 dB at 2:27, −23.3 dB at 2:28 and −17.0 dB at 2:30; the 5-second table shows −28.3 dB (2:25) and −16.1 dB (2:30), with onsets per second 0.4 to 3.2; boundary at 2:28 (novelty 0.30). A forceful chord heralding the return: Philharmonia guide.

cues.title: Louder and brighter again
cues.text: From 2:45 to 3:00 the wild music is loud and bright again, near −11 dB and about 1,300 to 1,900 Hz. Listen for the same earthy rushes as in the opening, now heading for the end.
cues.evidence: Relative level −12.0 dB (2:45), −11.2 (2:50), −10.9 (2:55), −13.3 (3:00); brightness 1,308, 1,491, 1,898 and 1,792 Hz; boundaries at 2:50 and 3:02 (novelty 0.43, 0.45). That the opening ideas return: Cleveland note and the movement’s A–B–A form.

cues.title: A rising rush, no break
cues.text: In the last twenty seconds the level climbs from about −21 dB to −12 dB and the brightness rises to 3,000 Hz. In the score this is a continuous rush of semiquavers that climbs to the last notes, which lead straight into the Great Gate.
cues.evidence: Relative level −20.4 dB (3:15), −21.6 (3:20), −19.8 (3:25), −12.5 (3:30); brightness 1,702 Hz (3:15) to 3,000 Hz (3:30); boundary at 3:14 (novelty 0.32). The detector counts only 0.0–0.2 onsets per second here; that is not the written note rate. The continuous semiquavers of bars 187–211, the rising close and the attacca on the last bar are in Lamm’s piano text (Mutopia, baba-allegro-molto.ily); the witch music running into the finale: Laki’s Cleveland Orchestra note and Wikipedia.

transitions.title: From a roar to a whisper
transitions.how: The wildest music stops and the level collapses by about twenty decibels. The tempo moves to Andante mosso, and the orchestra gives the ghoulish middle to a fluid flute, an enigmatic bassoon and double bass line, harp, celesta and shivering strings. The join is a cut; nothing prepares it harmonically. The clock’s ticking and the witch’s hut are suddenly close by.
transitions.evidence: Boundary at 1:08 (novelty 1.00); relative level −13.0 dB (1:05) to −33.6 dB (1:10), then −26 to −34 dB to 2:25. The flute, bassoon and double bass, harp, celesta and strings: Philharmonia guide; the Andante mosso mark is in the title.

transitions.title: One chord ends the hush
transitions.how: After more than a minute at the edge of silence, a forceful orchestral chord at about 2:28 raises the level by roughly seventeen decibels within three seconds and the strident material returns. The tempo is again fast: the title’s Allegro molto. The return reverses the cut that began the middle section, so the movement’s two halves are joined by two sudden changes of level.
transitions.evidence: A 1-second pass gives −34.1 dB at 2:27, −23.3 dB at 2:28 and −17.0 dB at 2:30; the 5-second table shows −28.3 dB (2:25) to −16.1 dB (2:30); onsets per second 0.4 to 3.2. A forceful chord heralding the return of the strident material: Philharmonia guide; the Allegro molto mark is in the title.

transitions.title: A rising rush leads into the Gate
transitions.how: The running music does not stop: the score keeps its rapid semiquavers through a closing run that climbs to the last notes, and the level in this recording rises from about −21 dB to −12 dB while the sound brightens to 3,000 Hz. The last bar is marked attacca, so the movement is joined, without a break, to the finale, The Great Gate of Kyiv, and the witch’s hut and the gate sound as one continuous span.
transitions.evidence: Boundary at 3:14 (novelty 0.32); relative level −20.4 dB (3:15) to −12.5 dB (3:30); brightness 1,702 Hz to 3,000 Hz; onsets per second 0.0 to 0.2, a detector figure and not the written note rate. The continuous semiquavers of bars 187–211, the rising close and the attacca are in Lamm’s piano text (Mutopia, baba-allegro-molto.ily); the coda leading without a break into the next movement: Wikipedia’s article and Laki’s Cleveland note.

fields.label: Work version
fields.value: Orchestral performance; Ravel’s 1922 orchestration is the probable version but is not named by any source
fields.note: Neither Commons, the Free Music Archive nor the Internet Archive names the orchestrator. The album’s four Promenades (none between “Samuel Goldenberg and Schmuÿle” and Limoges) match Ravel’s layout, and a 2015 Commons talk-page comment calls the recording Ravel’s orchestration of a rather poor Skidmore performance. The commenter gives no source. Instrument names in the listening notes follow Ravel’s scoring conditionally, as the introduction says; the audio report does not identify instruments.

fields.label: Recorded
fields.note: No session date is documented. The Internet Archive item says “date unknown, 2008 at the latest”; the Free Music Archive lists the album as released 6 April 2009; this file was uploaded to Commons on 2008-01-21. None of these is a recording date.

fields.label: Place
fields.note: No venue is documented. The Free Music Archive biography describes the orchestra as a semi-professional ensemble of Skidmore students and regional professionals; this is not a recording location.

fields.label: Composition rights
fields.value: Mussorgsky’s piano suite (he died in 1881) is public domain; Commons marks the music PD-old-100. An orchestration is a separate work with its own term and is not cleared here.
fields.note: The Commons notice covers Mussorgsky’s music only. If the version is Ravel’s, his orchestration is not assessed in this dossier.

fields.label: Recording rights
fields.value: Rule 1 — recording release: PD-author public-domain dedication by Musopen, with Wikimedia VRTS permission ticket 2008012110017088.
fields.note: The file description applies PD-author|Musopen to the recording separately from PD-old-100 for the music, and cites the VRTS ticket; the page is in “Items with VRTS permission confirmed”. Musopen’s reproduced policy says the music is public domain with no restrictions; its requests not to sell the recordings and to credit Musopen are courtesy requests, not a non-commercial licence. The Internet Archive copy of the first Promenade is marked CC0 1.0. Session date is not needed for this route.

composer.epithet: He made Russian speech, public crowds and the noises of ordinary life determine the shape of opera.
facts: Piano with Anton Gerke; composition informally with Mily Balakirev; no conservatory education
Guards officer until 1858; civil servant, including work in the Forestry Department
Balakirev, Borodin, Cui and Rimsky-Korsakov; the critic Vladimir Stasov
Operas, dramatic songs and piano music; many works unfinished or published in other composers’ revisions
composer.background:
Mussorgsky grew up on his family’s estate at Karevo, where his mother taught him the piano and his nurse supplied stories that he later associated with his earliest improvisations. The household belonged to the landowning class. The peasant voices he eventually put into songs and operas came from another social world. Sent to Saint Petersburg for schooling, he studied piano with Anton Gerke and entered the School of Guards Cadets in 1852. In 1856 he joined the Preobrazhensky Regiment. His first published piano piece, a polka, belonged to the drawing room.

Meeting Dargomyzhsky and then Balakirev redirected that education. Balakirev taught through playing, criticism and the examination of scores. Mussorgsky left the army in 1858, but composing did not provide a living. The emancipation of the serfs in 1861 disrupted the estate income on which his family depended, and he eventually took civil-service posts. The group later called the Five brought together different professions and musical methods: Borodin was a chemist, Cui a military engineer, Rimsky-Korsakov a naval officer. Their shared opposition to imported academic authority concealed substantial musical disagreements.
